desc:
There are several piles of stones; piles[i] is the number of stones in pile i. In one operation you choose a pile with p stones and throw away floor(p / 2) of them, so ceil(p / 2) stones stay in that pile. The same pile may be chosen again in later operations.

Perform exactly k operations (an operation on a pile with a single stone changes nothing) and return the smallest possible total number of stones left.

piles = [5, 4, 9], k = 2
9 -> 5 gives [5, 4, 5]
5 -> 3 gives [3, 4, 5]   total = 12
hints: An operation removes more stones from a big pile than from a small one. Which pile should the very first operation use?
Always halve the pile that is currently the largest: the number of stones it removes, floor(p / 2), never decreases with p.
You need to repeatedly find and update the maximum. A max-heap does that in O(log n); Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated sizes.
editorial: The gain of one operation on a pile of size p is floor(p / 2), which grows with p. Halving a pile also never makes another pile's gain bigger. So at every step the best move is to halve the current largest pile; an exchange argument shows that any plan that halves a smaller pile first can swap it for the larger one without losing stones.

Keep all piles in a max-heap. Repeat k times: look at the top, stop early if it is 1 (nothing can shrink any more), otherwise replace it by (top + 1) // 2. The answer is the sum of what is left in the heap.
Each operation costs O(log n), so the total is O((n + k) log n). Because a pile reaches 1 after about 14 halvings for piles up to 10,000, the loop stops after at most about 14 n steps.
